title: Buttercream colour blending
subtitle: ombre and watercolour effects on cake sides using palette knife and scraper
excerpt: Colour-blended buttercream creates a graduated or watercolour effect by applying two or more shades to the side of a cake and then blending them with a scraper in a single pass. The technique requires each colour to be applied as a distinct patch before scraping, so the blending happens in one controlled movement rather than by mixing the colours in the bowl first.
sourceNotes: Ombre buttercream techniques emerged in the US cake decorating community around 2012 to 2013 and spread globally via social media, becoming a standard repertoire technique for home bakers. The watercolour variant (using a palette knife to blend colours on the chilled crumb coat before scraping) developed later as a more expressive, less uniform alternative. Both use the same fundamental principle of applying separate colour patches and blending once.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Apply colouring and blend the day before serving. Refrigerate and allow to come to room temperature before serving.

glossaryTerms.definition: A graduated buttercream finish where the colour transitions from light at the top to dark at the base, or through multiple shades. The effect is created by applying colour patches and blending in one scraper pass, not by tinting buttercream to every shade individually.

content.text: Colour-blended buttercream works by relying on the scraper to do the blending, not your hand. Divide your base buttercream into portions and colour each separately. Apply them as distinct horizontal bands around the crumb-coated cake, then scrape once: the colours merge at their boundaries into a smooth
transition. For the watercolour effect, blend patches loosely with a palette knife before scraping.
Apply a crumb coat of plain white or pale buttercream and refrigerate for 30 minutes until firm. A clean, firm crumb coat prevents the top coat colours from picking up crumbs and muddying the blend.

Divide the buttercream into two to four portions depending on how many shades you want. Use gel food colouring: liquid colouring changes the buttercream's consistency. Mix each portion separately, starting with a small amount of colouring and working up. For an ombre, plan the shades as a sequence (white, pale pink, medium pink, deep rose); for a watercolour effect, the shades can be more varied.

Place the crumb-coated cake on the turntable. Using a palette knife or piping bag, apply each shade to the side of the cake in horizontal bands: the darkest colour at the base, the lightest at the top for a classic ombre, or any order you choose. Each band should overlap its neighbours by about 1 cm. Apply them thicker than the final result will be: you need material for the scraper to remove. Spread a dab of the lightest shade across the top of the cake.

Hold the bench scraper at a 90° angle against the side of the cake and spin the turntable smoothly in one complete rotation. The scraper removes the excess and blends the boundaries between shades as it passes. Do not go back over a section you have already scraped: each additional pass removes more colour and muddies the transition. If you need to correct a section, add a little more buttercream at the boundary and take one more single scraper pass.

For a looser, more expressive effect, use a palette knife to dab and blend patches of different shades directly onto the crumb coat, overlapping them irregularly. Some areas should show the bare crumb coat through. Then scrape the whole side in one pass: the pale crumb coat showing through acts as the lightest tone, and the scraper pulls the colours into each other where they overlap. The result is less uniform than ombre but more textured and painterly.
